title: How Unitree's Kung Fu Robot Learned to Fight
description:
Unitree says its new H2-X robot's kung fu is real: in its launch video (21 Oct 2026) the robot flips over a car, kicks dents into doors and "guards" a woman from a knife in its launch video (21 Oct 2026), and Unitree labels the footage "Real Footage Throughout No Speed-Up". Robots like it start by copying a person's motion, joint by joint, then practise it as thousands of virtual copies in a simulator, falling over until the move works. Unitree's own public training code (unitree_rl_gym) trains 4,096 simulated robots at once by default (its example tasks are walking), and in that code the controller acts every 0.02 seconds (50 times a second). We don't know H2-X's exact training pipeline. But the video's own small print says the "approximately 8 hours" of endurance is for standing, and labels the knife scene a "Security Demonstration".

Footage: Unitree Robotics, "Unitree Introducing: H2-X Kung Fu Legend Guardian" (YouTube, 21 Oct 2026), used in short clips under our commentary, slowed with frame interpolation: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y3zb4o47yqA
The simulator scenes and the balance shot are our own 3D illustration, not Unitree footage.

Sources:
Unitree's training code (Train > Play > Sim2Sim > Sim2Real; num_envs = 4096; sim dt 0.005 s x decimation 4): https://github.com/unitreerobotics/unitree_rl_gym
KungfuBot, how human kung fu motion is retargeted and learned on a Unitree G1 (NeurIPS 2025): https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.12851
H2-X specs and price not yet published (BigGo Finance): https://finance.biggo.com/news/b25f76b1-9b05-4d74-9d7d-f3df2163154c

title: Tesla Showed a Flying Car. Then Its Profit Fell 43%
description:
Six days after Tesla's flying-Roadster demo (15 Oct 2026), its Q3 2026 results (21 Oct) showed GAAP net income down 43%, from $1.37B to $787M. But gross profit rose about 9% ($5.05B to $5.49B). The difference is spending: research and development rose 69% in a year ($1.63B to $2.76B), and Tesla's own filing puts the rise in operating expenses down to "SI and other R&D projects, SBC (including 2025 CEO Performance Award) and SG&A" (SI is Tesla's term for "Super Intelligence"; SBC is stock-based compensation). The regulatory credits Tesla sells to other carmakers fell from $417M to $113M (about three quarters). Leave out stock-based pay and a few other items, and Tesla's own non-GAAP net income fell about 4% ($1.77B to $1.70B). All figures are from Tesla's Q3 2026 Update; the percentages are our arithmetic.

Footage: Tesla, "The Ramp | Roadster" and "The Kickflip | Roadster" and "The 0-60 | Roadster" (YouTube, 16 Oct 2026), slowed with frame interpolation, used in short clips under our commentary.

Source:
Tesla Q3 2026 Update (Form 8-K, exhibit 99.1, 21 Oct 2026): https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1318605/000162828026066738/exhibit9914.htm

title: How the Flying Tesla Roadster Actually Works
description:
Tesla's new Roadster hung upside down on a ramp, flipped over a row of trucks and hit 60 mph in 0.81 seconds at its 15 October 2026 demo. Here's how each trick actually works, what the numbers really say, and what Tesla's own contract and filings add.

Chapters
0:00 Upside down and not falling
0:26 The second machine: SpaceX-style jets
1:06 0.81 seconds, on Tesla's own stopwatch
1:46 Seconds in the air, hours to refill
2:35 The fan car that won once and vanished
3:14 Is the flying Roadster legal?
3:53 What $250,000 buys you
4:23 The bill: profit down 43%
4:54 Verdict: a vacuum cleaner and a very short rocket

What we found
- The hang: fans pull the air from under the car while skirts seal the gap; Tesla says the push reaches up to twice the car's weight, even standing still.
- The jets: two carbon-wrapped tanks (about 250 kg of compressed gas) feed 10 nozzles; the four rear nozzles give over 80 kN.
- 0.81 s was Tesla's own timing; nobody outside Tesla has timed the car yet.
- By our estimate the rear nozzles at full power would empty the tanks in about two seconds; a refill takes 2-6 hours on a nitrogen rig today (Lars Moravy to Top Gear).
- The trick isn't new: the Chaparral 2J (1970) and Brabham BT46B (1978) used fans, and the McMurtry Spéirling drove upside down in 2025.
- The FAA says the car isn't an aircraft; Tesla's own site says the Rocket version isn't approved for public roads.
- Tesla's US reservation agreement says it can't guarantee "if" the car will be delivered.
- Six days later, Tesla's Q3 2026 GAAP net income was down 43% (adjusted, about 4%), and its own filing lists the Roadster as "Design development".

Footage: Tesla, "The Ramp", "The Kickflip" and "The 0-60" (YouTube, 16 Oct 2026), used in short clips under our commentary and diagrams, some slowed with frame interpolation. The x-ray, tank and drop scenes are our own 3D illustrations, not Tesla footage.
